utterances.text: I'm going to answer your question, judge, but what your question is -- what you're saying is that it transpires from the transcript that supposedly Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Bubic came to an agreement that rather than proceeding with the interview, the interviewee at the time should have the opportunity to consult with his lawyer. Well, that is kind of amazing to me since they didn't care if he consulted with his lawyer before they started interviewing him when they knew he had a lawyer but that's not the issue, Judge That's not the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a submission and it is not related to either coercion or voluntariness in any case. I think we need to bring this to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right may I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to say, Your Honours, it's clear that he is struggling to even articulate a basis of why this is relevant which shows it's purely and nothing else but a fishing expedition. He has not laid out any good faith basis whatsoever to go into this area. He hasn't talked to the other party there, the attorney, there is something very wrong any way -- I'll try to slow down, without a good faith basis to start delving into the discussions between prosecutors and Defence attorneys which occur at virtually every meeting, and I think we should end it now. He has not been able to articulate a single rational basis. He can't even -- he's reading and trying to think of something to say. It's obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the last word, Mr. Meek, and then we decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's funny and kind of amusing that they are so upset that they don't want me to ask this question, and the only question is did Mr. McCloskey tell you what they talked about, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Meek. We see absolutely no connection at all between your question and the aspects of coercion and voluntariness which was not raised by the party who is more -- most interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So if I understand well, then, I can't ask this witness whose idea was it to teak the break or if Mr. McCloskey and he discussed what they talked about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can put that question, but I think one of them has been already put and answered. And he told you, I don't know, I don't recall. But you're free to ask both questions again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who wanted to take the break and decided to, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall who instigated the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you were with Mr. McCloskey for a few days after this interview, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you and he discuss what had been talked about with Mr. Bubic?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you introduce yourself to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My name is Natacha Fauveau Ivanovic and I appear it here for General Miletic. I will have very few questions for you, in fact. You spoke yesterday and today on many occasions about the caution that you gave to the interviewee. And that involved information about his rights. Do you remember that in the course of that interview, Mr. Borovcanin was cautioned several times that it was very important for him to tell the truth? I'm talking about the interview of the 20th of February.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're asking me to confirm, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you look at page 34? I'm not sure it's the same number of the page in your version, I'm not sure we have the same version.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the first interview, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the transcript of the 20th of February. That should be the page ERN number 0068862.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you read what is between lines 4 and 13, sorry, 14?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We are evaluating everything you tell us and it's very important for you to tell us the whole truth because we want to consider that as we evaluate your situation, we don't view you as the -- as we may view Mladic and Krstic and the major commanders in this case, and if you can be open with us and honest with us, we will be able to talk to you and your lawyer and consider the best way to handle your situation. But if we find that you're evading us or protecting other people then we'll just have to do our duty and just continue as without your cooperation. "And we have heard throughout from General Krstic and others blaming it on General Mladic, blaming it on the people that are in Serbia, this kind of thing. So please I'll just stop now so you can think about how important this is to tell us the whole truth, and I thank you for everything you've said so far and the documents you brought." Is that as far as you wanted me to --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I would like to know this: You certainly had the opportunity to interview more than one person within the framework of investigations at this Tribunal and in your national police force. Is it customary to tell a person who has the status of suspect that it is very important to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my domestic jurisdiction we would tell somebody they should tell us the truth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To a person who has the status of suspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I think that was included in your question, previous question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would agree, Mr. President, but what confuses me a little is that the witness answered "we would tell somebody." That's why I wanted to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Fauveau. And would that "somebody," you used the word "somebody," would that include a suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before the Tribunal, in the Tribunal, are you in the habit of telling suspects that -- or were you in the habit of telling suspects that it is important for them to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm just not again clear how this is relevant or how this goes to one of the issues in this case, if she can tie it in somehow because it's not clear to me whatsoever. I mean, she's read out the portion of the transcript, we've gone over some of this ground. Again there has been no allegation whatsoever of any coercion or improperness, so I don't know where it's going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls but Madam Fauveau would you like to comments on that? That can be tied up, Mr. Nicholls. I mean, so I frankly I don't think you need to explain. In our mind it's quite clear that it could be tied up, basically that that could be interpreted by the interviewee as a kind of pressure. This is what she is after.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Kindly answer the question, if you need Madam Fauveau to repeat it, then I'm sure she will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if I could have the question again, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, please. I can actually read it. The question was the following [Microphone not activated]. I'm sorry. "In the Tribunal, are you in the habit of telling suspects or were you in the habit of telling suspects that it is important for them to tell the truth?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the record as to how many times I used that phrase. I would imagine I have used it previously or since in interviews at the Tribunal, but it would be on record. I would expect I probably have used it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you used that phrase, is it because you suspect that the person across the table from you is not telling you the truth?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just be clear on one thing? I think the passage you're referring to is not something that I actually said, but I'm still happy to answer the question about what I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You are perfectly right. These words here are not yours. But I'm not going to go into that. My question is generally, it doesn't concern this specific occasion only. When you remind somebody that it's important for them to tell the truth, is it because there is a suspicion in your mind that they are not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It will depend on the circumstances. I'm just reiterating what I consider to be a valid point whenever I would do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I have to admit I don't really understand why is it necessary to remind somebody to tell the truth if you have no suspicions whatsoever. What is the purpose, then?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's to make sure that they understand that that is what is hoped for from the interview to establish the truth. Not everybody that is interviewed does tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I in my records, I have no indication that anyone else wishes to cross-examine the witness. If I am not right or the situation has changed, please let me know. No? Mr. Nicholls, do you wish to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were asked one question on cross-examination by my friend regarding when the tapes from the second interview would have been provided to Borovcanin, and my friend stated that he did not receive them until he arrived at The Hague. Are you aware of or do you recall when it was that Mr. Borovcanin became a fugitive and failed to appear at his appointment to voluntarily surrender?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall the exact date, but I am aware that there was a further meeting with Mr. Borovcanin after these interviews and I was not present. It was a different investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I have one moment? [Prosecution counsel confer]?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing further now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. One moment. I need to consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't have questions or anything, but just to clarify this issue that Mr. Nicholls has just raised, can we be more specific about the date when the Prosecution believes that Mr. Borovcanin became fugitive? Because I would like to state that it was in September, and the interviews took place in August so just -- in March, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In March. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Graham, I have one short question for you. I would take it that you are familiar with what is spelled out in our Rule 42, the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, relating to the rights of suspects during investigations and in paragraph (A)(iii), the rule requires that the suspect is informed prior to questioning in a language that he or she understands that he or she has a right to remain silent and to be cautioned that any statement the suspect makes shall be recorded and may be used in evidence. These are the exact words used in our rules. You will notice that the rule or the subparagraph does not state "that may be used against him or her in evidence or in a trial" or the words that you use yourself. Our question to you or my question to you is the following: If Rule 42 does not contemplate the use, the specific use, of those words, why did you use them? Why did you each time you cautioned the interviewee, you used the words "against you"?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was on the pro forma document that I had been provided with that had been used by team members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know that aide-memoire you referred to still exists or not?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cannot be certain it was an identical one, but I'm aware that there is one that is very similar with that wording on, and I think the Prosecution are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Graham, I think we can safely bring your testimony to an end here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber and the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and we also wish you a safe journey back home. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before Mr. Graham is completely released can I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To you. It's procedural, Your Honour. This hearing --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Could the witness leave the courtroom, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know what this is, and I'd like him to leave the courtroom, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Graham.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't envisage the need to bring him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, Your Honour. That's why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's why I asked that he not be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's simply this, Your Honour, this hearing was as you know, limited to a specific topic which we've thrashed out. During the interview, Mr. Borovcanin brought documents to the interview which he shared, the OTP brought documents which were used in the interview, and documents were generated during the interview drawings and charts. In addition on the second interview, Mr. Borovcanin brought a videotape and the OTP brought a DVD and those were viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not something I could get into in this hearing. However, if it turns out that the interview is admissible regardless of against whom at this point, I would want to do a brief direct rather than bringing him back, in order to lay the foundation for the admissibility of those documents which are on our 65 ter list. That's all I have to say. I don't know if it would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No, no. Obviously you had discussed this with some members of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, it may be possible to stipulate. I don't know and we could talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Does anyone wish to comment on that? Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm quite loath to go before Mr. Lazarevic on this particular subject. I don't know whether he has any submissions. But yes, I do, Your Honour, because the Chamber in our submission first of all has to ascertain whether this interview is admissible against Mr. Borovcanin. Secondly, the Chamber will then need to decide whether it's admissible against -- if the answer to question one is yes, is it admissible against the six other accused? If the answer to that is yes, then I for one on behalf of General Gvero, would like to ask him some general questions about one or two things that have occurred in the interview and also the other material. Now, let me make our position plain. Regrettable as it may seem, we contend that that cannot be done until the Trial Chamber has ruled on both of those difficult questions, and so this witness in our submission will have to return to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Lazarevic, would you like to comment on Mr. Nicholls' --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, basically my position is exactly the same as Mr. Josse and very finely pointed out. But there is one issue. I cannot exclude the possibility that we might stipulate something with the Prosecution. However, there are some problems because it seems that some part of documents that were used during this interview are missing, I don't know for what reason, and I would like to have further discussion and then follow -- but I think this should follow the decision on the admittance of the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Anyone else? None? Please let us confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It didn't take us much to disagree with you, Mr. Nicholls, and agree instead with Mr. Josse and Mr. Lazarevic. It's obvious that everything is predicated on the first two decisions to be taken, that is admissibility, first vis-a-vis Mr. Borovcanin, second admissibility vis-a-vis the other accused, and it would seem unavoidable that if the statement is admitted, questions will need to be asked on the content, on the rest of the contents of the statement which are not related to voluntariness. So I think the return of Mr. Graham is unavoidable, and I think he's only got to fly from Manchester to here so let's not make a mountain out of a mole hill. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I might have been overly optimistic on the speed of your decision on the first issue. I didn't know how long it would take. I can see Mr. Josse's points, but what I was referring to at least regarding the first step, Mr. Borovcanin, that that might be something that would -- that could be resolved. And then when we got to the second step we could see if more questions were needed. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that change anything, Mr. Josse, Mr. Lazarevic, or do you retain -- stick by your position? I don't think it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's the position. Now, we have, before we return to the courtroom during the break discussed a little bit what's going to happen next. And our idea is that or our conviction is that you would probably need to make submissions on what has -- on what has happened yesterday and today. There are of course two options. If you are prepared to make oral submissions today, we would then ask you to stand up and do so. But we understand that this could reach you as a surprise because there was no indication that we would finish so early today. So the other possibility is that you may wish to make your submissions in writing, in which case, of course, you would find us accepting that. So there is the Prosecution, I suppose, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Meek, that are mostly interested, but I'm not excluding by any means any of the other Defence teams if in spite of not having cross-examined the witness they wish to make submissions. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a creature of old habit, but this is a simple issue. There is no major complicated law. I would like for to us argue it and Defence to argue it today and have it done with and perhaps you can deliberate on it while Mr. Graham is still here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Lazarevic, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I have five minutes? Maybe all of the counsel because it's not related only to myself, but if we could have 10 to 15 minutes to discuss this issue with our clients?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Meek, that applies -- Mr. Lazarevic. That applies to you, Mr. Meek, and to any other Defence counsel that wishes to participate in these. For the time being keep him here so that we decide whether we are going to have oral submissions today or written submissions later. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One other option, Your Honour, I would prefer -- I'm ready. I'd prefer to do oral submissions. If we can just do them now if everybody else is ready, or if not I would rather just do oral submissions tomorrow rather than do this in writing because as Mr. McCloskey says I think it's pretty simple, and we can probably do it quite quickly. Whether it's today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. We'll have ten minutes will suffice, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 5.07 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Subject of course to Your Honours' decision, during the break we've talked and the parties agree that it would be preferable to just make arguments tomorrow. That's what everybody would like to do, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 1, all this is premised on our releasing the witness, first and foremost, agreed? I hear nothing against. All right. Number 2, who wishes to make oral submissions tomorrow? Let's start from you, Mr. Nicholls. Will you be making some oral submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For how long? How much time do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll be probably 20 minutes or less, 20 minutes maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 20 minutes. Okay. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I will make an oral submission, and I believe that 35 maybe minutes would be a sufficient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will make submissions, and I would say 20, 25 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. We will not make any submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyone else thinks they would make submissions, you would make submissions? No. So we are talking of one hour and 20 minutes. We will reduce that to one hour and please arrange amongst yourselves how you distribute the time. Mr. Lazarevic, being the promoter of the whole matter, will go first. Mr. Meek, you will go second. Mr. Nicholls, you will go third. You should allow yourselves, then, some time for a reply, a response, if there is a need for them, but all this needs to be completed in one hour. We will sit tomorrow from 3.30 to 4.30. All right? Thank you. Any further submissions on anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just confirm, and that will conclude the sittings this side of the recess; is that right, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. Of course, between today and Friday, we will be working intensively on some outstanding motions including the joinder motion, which hopefully will be concluded and handed down tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In writing, presumably, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honours, just to be clear, I take it we can now talk to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're starting to make me suspect that I am not clear at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a new issue. You've been very clear. I just take it that now the OTP can speak with Mr. Graham again because this issue is done. Just on the topic of -- now the substance, meaning these various exhibits that we would -- that we -- if there is no stipulation that we will try to put in with him and that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't pre-empt issues, because whether Mr. Graham will return to testify again depends on whether the Borovcanin -- alleged Borovcanin statement will be admitted in evidence vis-a-vis Mr. Borovcanin and/or vis-a-vis the six other accused. If it's not admitted, there won't be any need for you to speak to Mr. Graham any further on the Borovcanin statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's just that normally we speak to the witness before he leaves, Your Honour. He's going back and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's another matter. [Microphone not activated] Is there any opposition from any of the Defence teams, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour by all means. I trust my colleagues from the Prosecution that they will not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for being pragmatic and constructive, Mr. Lazarevic. So I think that concludes. Later on in the week you should expect two or three decisions, if not four, and then we will adjourn until August the 21st, not the 20th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
